# MSW (Mock Service Worker)

**IMPORTANT:** Your training data about `msw` may be outdated or incorrect — MSW v2 completely removed the `rest` namespace, `res(ctx.*)` response composition, and `(req, res, ctx)` resolver signature. MSW v3 is ESM-only and requires Node.js >=22 and TypeScript >=5.9. Always rely on this skill's rule files and the project's actual source code as the source of truth. Do not fall back on memorized v1 or v2 patterns when they conflict with the retrieved reference.

## When to Use MSW

MSW is for **API mocking at the network level** — intercepting HTTP, GraphQL, Server-Sent Events (`sse`) and WebSocket (`ws`) traffic in tests, Storybook, and local development without modifying application code.

| Need | Recommended Tool |
|------|-----------------|
| Test API integration (React, Vue, Node) | **MSW** |
| Storybook API mocking | **MSW** (browser worker) |
| Local development without backend | **MSW** (browser worker) |
| Unit testing pure functions | Plain test doubles |
| E2E testing real APIs | Playwright/Cypress network interception |
| Mocking module internals | `vi.mock()` / `jest.mock()` |

## Quick Reference

```typescript
// Imports
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'
import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'
import { sse } from 'msw/sse'
import { ws } from 'msw/ws'
import { delay } from 'msw/utils/delay'
import { bypass } from 'msw/utils/bypass'
import { passthrough } from 'msw/utils/passthrough'
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node'     // tests, SSR
import { setupWorker } from 'msw/browser'  // Storybook, dev
// React Native: import { setupServer } from '@msw/react-native'

// Handler
http.get('/api/user/:id', async ({ request, params, cookies }) => {
  return HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, name: 'John' })
})

// Server lifecycle (tests)
beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: 'error' }))
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())
afterAll(() => server.close())

// Per-test override
server.use(
  http.get('/api/user/:id', () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }))
)

// Concurrent test isolation
it.concurrent('name', server.boundary(async () => {
  server.use(/* scoped overrides */)
}))
```

## v1 to v2 Migration Quick Reference

| v1 | v2 |
|----|-----|
| `import { rest } from 'msw'` | `import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw'` |
| `rest.get(url, resolver)` | `http.get(url, resolver)` |
| `(req, res, ctx) => res(ctx.json(data))` | `() => HttpResponse.json(data)` |
| `req.params` | `params` from resolver info |
| `req.body` | `await request.json()` |
| `req.cookies` | `cookies` from resolver info |
| `res.once(...)` | `http.get(url, resolver, { once: true })` |
| `res.networkError()` | `HttpResponse.error()` |
| `ctx.delay(ms)` | `await delay(ms)` |
| `ctx.data({ user })` | `HttpResponse.json({ data: { user } })` |

## v2 to v3 Migration Quick Reference

MSW 3.0.0 is **ESM-only** and requires **Node.js >=22** and **TypeScript >=5.9** (v6/v7 also supported). The headline change: handlers and utilities are imported from subpath entrypoints instead of the package root. `msw/graphql` needs the optional peer dependency `graphql` (>=16) installed. See `references/migration-v2-to-v3.md` for the complete guide (and the official codemods).

| v2 | v3 |
|----|-----|
| `import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw'` | `import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'` |
| `import { graphql } from 'msw'` | `import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'` |
| `import { ws } from 'msw'` / `import { sse } from 'msw'` | `msw/ws` / `msw/sse` |
| `import { delay } from 'msw'` | `import { delay } from 'msw/utils/delay'` |
| `import { bypass, passthrough } from 'msw'` | `msw/utils/bypass`, `msw/utils/passthrough` |
| `graphql.query(...)` on the namespace | Removed — link-first: `graphql.link(url).query(...)` |
| `import { setupServer } from 'msw/native'` | `@msw/react-native` package replaces the `msw/native` entrypoint |
| `handleRequest()` | Removed — use `getResponse()` (or experimental `defineNetwork()` for custom networks) |
| `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` | `onUnhandledFrame: 'error'` — covers requests AND WebSocket connections. Plain JavaScript ignores a leftover `onUnhandledRequest`, so the default `'warn'` applies |
| Custom callback `(request, print)` | Single `{ frame, defaults }` object; narrow with `frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame` (`msw/experimental`), call `defaults.warn()` |
| `server.events.on('connection', ...)` | `server.events.on('websocket:connection', ...)` — life-cycle API only; the `ws` link's own `addEventListener('connection')` keeps its name |
| `GraphQLLinkHandlers` type | Renamed to `GraphQLLink` |
| `LifeCycleEventsMap` from `msw` | Per-protocol maps (`HttpNetworkFrameEventMap`, `WebSocketNetworkFrameEventMap`) from `msw/experimental` |
| `worker.stop()` returns void | Returns a Promise — `await worker.stop()` for in-flight critical scenarios |
| `:segments+` and `:path*` give an array (`['user', 'privacy']`) | One string with slashes (`'user/privacy'`). The type still allows an array, so TypeScript does not report `.join()` on it |
| RegExp tokens in a string predicate (`'/user/:id(\\d+)'`) | Match no request. Use a `RegExp` predicate |

New in v3: `msw/vite` plugin (serves the worker script — no more copying `mockServiceWorker.js` into public), GraphQL v17 and link-first subscriptions, the WebSocket Extension API, page-navigation and form-submission interception, passthrough request-header modification, and per-utility `msw/utils/*` modules for smaller bundles.

# MSW Skill

Created by **[Anivar Aravind](https://anivar.net)**

An AI agent skill for writing, reviewing, and debugging MSW (Mock Service Worker) v3 handlers, server setup, and test patterns with modern best practices.

## The Problem

AI agents often generate outdated MSW v1 patterns — `rest.get()` instead of `http.get()`, `res(ctx.json(...))` instead of `HttpResponse.json()`, `(req, res, ctx)` instead of `({ request, params })` — and miss critical testing best practices like `server.boundary()` for concurrent tests, `onUnhandledFrame: 'error'`, and proper lifecycle hook setup. These produce code that fails to compile or silently misbehaves at runtime.

## This Solution

20 rules with incorrect/correct code examples that teach agents MSW v3's actual API, handler design, server lifecycle, response construction, testing patterns, GraphQL usage, and v1-to-v2 and v2-to-v3 migration. Each rule targets a specific mistake and shows exactly how to fix it.

## 1.2.2

Checked against **msw 3.0.3** on Node.js 26.12.1, with the same handlers run on **msw 2.15.0** for comparison.

### Added — the v2-to-v3 migration guide missed two breaking changes

- **A repeating path parameter is one string in v3.** `/settings/:segments+` on `/settings/user/privacy` gives `['user', 'privacy']` on msw 2.15.0 and `'user/privacy'` on msw 3.0.3. The `PathParams` type still allows an array, so `params.segments.join('/')` type-checks and then throws. `references/migration-v2-to-v3.md` and the `SKILL.md` migration table now say so and give code that works on both versions.
- **RegExp tokens in a string predicate no longer match.** `'/user/:id(\\d+)'` matched `/user/123` on msw 2.15.0 and matches no request on msw 3.0.3. The migration guide, its checklist, the `SKILL.md` table and `references/handler-api.md` now point to a `RegExp` predicate.

Both changes come from the move to the `@msw/url` matcher in msw 3.0.0. The msw path-parameters docs page still shows arrays.

## 1.2.1

Checked against **msw 3.0.3** on Node.js 26. Every changed example was type-checked with TypeScript 5.9 in strict mode, and every changed behaviour claim was executed against msw 3.0.3.

### Corrected — the skill taught something untrue

- **The GraphQL response-shape rule used the removed namespace API.** The Correct example in `rules/graphql-response-shape.md` called `graphql.query()`, which v3 does not have. It now defines the operations on `graphql.link('/graphql')`. The `once` example in `references/handler-api.md` had the same defect.
- **The GraphQL scope rule described v2.** `rules/graphql-scope-with-link.md` showed `graphql.query()` as the unscoped case. In v3 every operation is on a link. The rule now shows that a wildcard or RegExp link (`'*'`, `'*/graphql'`, `/graphql$/`) answers the same operation on two endpoints, and that one exact link per API does not. Executed against two endpoints.
- **`matchRequestUrl` and `PathParams` are not exported from `msw/http`.** That entrypoint exports only `http`, `HttpResponse`, `HttpHandler` and `HttpMethods`. `references/handler-api.md` now imports both from `msw`. Executed: the custom predicate and the standalone call return `{ matches, params }`.
- **`frame.protocol === 'http'` does not narrow `frame.data`** (TS18046 in strict mode). The custom `onUnhandledFrame` examples now narrow with `frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame` from `msw/experimental` (`references/server-api.md`, `references/migration-v2-to-v3.md`, `SKILL.md`). Executed: asset requests are skipped and other requests reach `defaults.warn()`.
- **The custom `onUnhandledFrame` callback takes one `{ frame, defaults }` object**, not `(request)` (`rules/test-unhandled-request.md`, `AGENTS.md`).
- **The import map sent every handler and utility to `'msw'`** (`rules/setup-import-paths.md`, `AGENTS.md`). It now gives the v3 subpaths.
- **Reading the body in `request:start` without `clone()` does not give the handler an empty body.** The handler lookup fails with `TypeError: unusable`, and the client receives a 500 response (`rules/request-clone-events.md`, `AGENTS.md`).
- **`onUnhandledFrame: 'error'` does not throw into the test.** It prints `[MSW] Error: intercepted a request without a matching request handler`, and the request rejects with `TypeError: fetch failed`. The default `'warn'` prints a warning; it is not silent (`rules/test-unhandled-request.md`, `references/server-api.md`, `references/anti-patterns.md`, `AGENTS.md`).
- **A native `Response` drops `Set-Cookie` only in the browser.** Node.js keeps the header, and the client receives it. `HttpResponse` stays the advice, because only it behaves the same in both environments (`rules/response-use-httpresponse.md`, `references/response-api.md`, `references/anti-patterns.md`, `SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md`).
- **The network-error message depends on the runtime.** The skill gave "Failed to fetch" as the message; Node.js says "fetch failed", and browsers differ. - **A native `Response.error()` also gives a network error.** The comparison table in `references/response-api.md` said "Not possible". Executed: both reject with `TypeError: fetch failed`.
- **Repeating path parameters arrive as one string in msw 3.0.3.** `:path*` and `:segments+` give `'a/b/c.txt'`, not an array. The docs and the type allow an array, so the wildcard example accepts both forms; its old `[].concat()` did not type-check (`references/handler-api.md`, `rules/handler-resolver-v2.md`, `references/migration-v1-to-v2.md`, `AGENTS.md`).

## HTTP Handlers

All methods on the `http` namespace:

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `http.get(predicate, resolver, options?)` | GET requests |
| `http.post(predicate, resolver, options?)` | POST requests |
| `http.put(predicate, resolver, options?)` | PUT requests |
| `http.patch(predicate, resolver, options?)` | PATCH requests |
| `http.delete(predicate, resolver, options?)` | DELETE requests |
| `http.head(predicate, resolver, options?)` | HEAD requests |
| `http.options(predicate, resolver, options?)` | OPTIONS requests |
| `http.all(predicate, resolver, options?)` | Any HTTP method |

### Signature

```text
http.get(
  predicate:
    | string
    | RegExp
    | ((args: { request: Request; cookies: Record<string, string> }) =>
        | boolean
        | { matches: boolean; params: Record<string, string | string[]> }),
  resolver: (info: {
    request: Request
    params: Record<string, string | string[]>
    cookies: Record<string, string>
    requestId: string
    finalize: (callback: () => void | Promise<void>) => void
  }) => Response | HttpResponse | undefined | void | Promise<...>,
  options?: { once?: boolean }
)
```

The predicate is a `string`, a `RegExp`, or a function — **not** a `URL` instance. Absolute URLs are supported, but as strings: `http.get('https://api.example.com/user', resolver)`. Passing `new URL(...)` is not a supported predicate type and throws when the handler is constructed.

## GraphQL Handlers

v3 is link-first: the `graphql` namespace no longer exposes `query`/`mutation`/`operation` directly — create a link per endpoint and define operations on it.

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `graphql.link(url)` | Create a scoped link for an endpoint (string, wildcard, or RegExp) |
| `link.query(predicate, resolver, options?)` | GraphQL queries on that link |
| `link.mutation(predicate, resolver, options?)` | GraphQL mutations on that link |
| `link.operation(resolver)` | Any GraphQL operation on that link |
| `link.subscription(predicate, resolver)` | GraphQL subscriptions (new in v3) — resolver gets a `subscription` object with `publish()` |

### Signature

```typescript
const api = graphql.link('https://api.example.com/graphql')
```

```text
api.query<Query, Variables>(
  predicate: string | RegExp | DocumentNode | TypedDocumentNode,
  resolver: (info: {
    query
    variables
    operationName
    request
    cookies
    requestId
    finalize
  }) => ...,
  options?: { once?: boolean }
)
```

### GraphQL predicates

```typescript
// Operation name — exact match
api.query('GetUser', resolver)

// RegExp — tested against the operation name
api.mutation(/user/i, resolver) // matches CreateUser and UpdateUser

// DocumentNode / TypedDocumentNode — from gql`...` or codegen
api.query(GetUserDocument, resolver)
```

### GraphQL Resolver Info

```typescript
api.query('GetUser', ({
  query,           // the GraphQL query sent from the client
  variables,       // Record<string, any> — query variables
  operationName,   // string — operation name
  request,         // Request — standard Fetch API Request
  cookies,         // Record<string, string>
  requestId,       // string
  finalize,        // (callback) => void — schedule cleanup after the resolver completes
}) => {
  return HttpResponse.json({ data: { user: { id: variables.id } } })
})
```

## URL Predicates

### String — Exact pathname match

```typescript
http.get('/api/user', resolver)
```

### String with params — Captures path parameters

```typescript
http.get('/api/user/:id', resolver)
```

A string predicate takes `:name`, `:name?`, `:name*`, `:name+` and `*`. It does not take RegExp
tokens: in msw 3.0.3, `'/api/user/:id(\\d+)'` matches no request. Use a `RegExp` predicate for that.

### Wildcard — Matches path prefix

```typescript
http.get('/api/*', resolver) // matches /api/anything
```

### Absolute URL — Full URL match

```typescript
http.get('https://api.example.com/user', resolver)
```

### RegExp — Pattern matching

```typescript
http.get(/\/api\/user\/\d+/, resolver)
```

### Custom function — Programmatic matching

The predicate function receives `request` and `cookies`, and returns a boolean:

```typescript
http.get(
  ({ request, cookies }) => {
    const url = new URL(request.url)
    return url.pathname.startsWith('/api') && url.searchParams.has('v')
  },
  resolver,
)
```

A boolean predicate does no path matching, so `params` in the resolver is always `{}`. To keep path-parameter parsing, return the extended result instead — an object of the shape `{ matches: boolean, params: Record<string, string | string[]> }` — and parse the params yourself with `matchRequestUrl()`:

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'
import { matchRequestUrl, type PathParams } from 'msw'

http.get<PathParams>(
  ({ request }) => {
    const url = new URL(request.url)

    return {
      matches: url.searchParams.has('mock'),
      // `.params` is required — matchRequestUrl returns { matches, params }.
      params: matchRequestUrl(url, 'https://api.example.com/user/:id').params ?? {},
    }
  },
  ({ params }) => HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id }),
)
```

## Path Parameters

### Single parameter

```typescript
http.get('/user/:id', ({ params }) => {
  const { id } = params // string
  return HttpResponse.json({ id })
})
```

### Multiple parameters

```typescript
http.get('/user/:userId/post/:postId', ({ params }) => {
  const { userId, postId } = params
  return HttpResponse.json({ userId, postId })
})
```

### Wildcard parameter

A bare `*` is an *unnamed* group, so there is no `params['*']` — reading it gives
`undefined`. Name the parameter instead, which is both readable and stable:

```typescript
http.get('/files/:path*', ({ params }) => {
  // msw 3.0.3 passes the matched segments as one string: 'a/b/c.txt'.
  // The docs and the type also allow an array, so accept both.
  const path = [params.path ?? []].flat().join('/')
  return HttpResponse.json({ path })
})
```

## Handler Options

### One-time handler

Automatically removed after the first matching request:

```typescript
http.get('/api/data', resolver, { once: true })
graphql.link('/graphql').query('GetUser', resolver, { once: true })
```

Useful for testing retry logic — first request fails, second succeeds:

```typescript
server.use(
  http.get('/api/data', () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }), { once: true })
)
// First request → 500 (one-time handler consumed)
// Second request → default handler responds
```

## matchRequestUrl Utility

Matches a URL against a path pattern and extracts path parameters. Its main use is inside a custom predicate function (see above), where MSW does not parse path parameters for you; it also works standalone.

```typescript
// matchRequestUrl is exported from the package root, not from 'msw/http'.
import { matchRequestUrl } from 'msw'

// Always returns an object — check `.matches`, never the object itself.
// A relative pattern is resolved against the document location, so outside a
// browser context match against an absolute pattern.
const match = matchRequestUrl(
  new URL('https://example.com/user/abc-123'),
  'https://example.com/user/:id',
)

if (match.matches) {
  console.log(match.params?.id) // 'abc-123'
}
```

A non-match returns `{ matches: false, params: {} }` — still a truthy object, so `if (match)` is unconditionally true.

## Resolver Cleanup with `finalize`

`finalize` is part of the resolver info on every namespace — `http.*`, `graphql.*`, `sse` and `ws`. It schedules cleanup to run after the request handler completes, which is what you need for side effects a resolver starts but does not own, such as intervals and timeouts on a stream:

```typescript
import { sse } from 'msw/sse'

sse('/ping', ({ client, finalize }) => {
  const interval = setInterval(() => client.send({ data: 'pong' }), 250)
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => client.close(), 1000)

  finalize(() => {
    clearInterval(interval)
    clearTimeout(timeout)
  })
})
```

Points to remember:

- The signature is `finalize(callback: () => Promise<void> | void): void`.
- It has no effect on the surrounding resolver's closure. You cannot await it, and it must not become a dependency of any of your request handler logic.
- Multiple `finalize()` calls run LIFO — the last registered callback runs first.
- Callbacks run even if the response resolver throws. Unhandled exceptions in them are collected into an `AggregateError` reported after all callbacks complete.

## WebSocket Handlers

`ws.link(url: string | URL | RegExp)` creates a link to a WebSocket endpoint. The `connection` event fires whenever a client opens a matching connection:

```typescript
import { ws } from 'msw/ws'

const chat = ws.link('wss://chat.example.com')

export const handlers = [
  chat.addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    client.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
      client.send(`echo: ${event.data}`)
    })
  }),
]
```

| Member | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `client.send(data)` | Send `string`, `Blob` or `ArrayBuffer` to the client |
| `client.close(code?, reason?)` | Close the client connection |
| `client.addEventListener(event, cb)` | Listen for `message`, `error`, `close` |
| `link.clients` | `Set` of all active client connections |
| `link.broadcast(data)` | Send to every connected client |
| `link.broadcastExcept(clients, data)` | Send to every client except those given |
| `server.connect()` | Connect to the actual server; without it the handler *is* the server |
| `server.send(data)` | Send data to the actual server |
| `server.addEventListener(event, cb)` | Listen for `open`, `message`, `error`, `close` on the real connection |

## Server-Sent Events Handlers

`sse(predicate, resolver)` intercepts `EventSource` connections. The resolver receives `client` (the intercepted `EventSource`) alongside the usual resolver info:

```typescript
import { sse } from 'msw/sse'

export const handlers = [
  sse<{ greeting: string }>('/api/events', ({ client }) => {
    client.send({ id: 'abc-123', event: 'greeting', data: 'Hello, John!' })
    client.close()
  }),
]
```

| Member | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `client.send({ id?, event?, data })` | Send an event to the client |
| `client.error()` | Error the underlying HTTP connection |
| `client.close()` | Gracefully close the underlying HTTP connection |
| `server.connect()` | Returns an `EventSource` to the actual server |

Once connected via `server.connect()`, all server events are forwarded to the client by default; call `event.preventDefault()` on a server event to stop it being forwarded.

See `rules/response-streaming.md` for when to use `sse()` versus a `ReadableStream` body.

# MSW v2 to v3 Migration Guide

MSW 3.0 (checked against 3.0.3) restructures the package entrypoints, makes GraphQL mocking link-first, and unifies the handling of unhandled requests and WebSocket connections. Official guide: https://mswjs.io/docs/migrations/2.x-to-3.x — MSW also ships **codemods** for the migration (see the official guide's "Codemods" link).

## Requirements

| Requirement | v2 | v3 |
|-------------|----|----|
| Module format | CJS + ESM | **ESM only** |
| Node.js | v18+ | **v22+** (v24 and v26 also supported; msw 3.0.3's `engines` field says `>=22.12.0`) |
| TypeScript | v4.7+ (msw 2.15.0 declares `>=4.8`) | **v5.9+** (v6.0 and v7.0 also supported) |

If your project still needs CommonJS, Node.js <22, or TypeScript <5.9, stay on `msw@2` (`^2.15.0`) until you can upgrade the toolchain.

## Imports — everything moves to subpaths

Request handlers, event handlers, and utilities are now exported from designated entrypoints instead of the package root. In msw 3.0.3 the root `msw` module still re-exports most of them (`http`, `HttpResponse`, `ws`, `sse`, `delay`, `bypass`, `passthrough`, `isCommonAssetRequest`), but not `graphql`, `setupServer` or `setupWorker`. Follow the subpaths: an import of `graphql` from `msw` breaks.

Before (v2):

```typescript
// @ts-expect-error msw 3 does not export graphql from the root; import it from 'msw/graphql'
import { http, HttpResponse, graphql, ws, sse, delay, bypass, passthrough } from 'msw'
```

After (v3):

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'
import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'
import { ws } from 'msw/ws'
import { sse } from 'msw/sse'
import { delay } from 'msw/utils/delay'
import { bypass } from 'msw/utils/bypass'
import { passthrough } from 'msw/utils/passthrough'
```

| Export | 2.x | 3.x |
|--------|-----|-----|
| `http`, `HttpResponse` | `msw` | `msw/http` |
| `graphql` | `msw` | `msw/graphql` |
| `ws` | `msw` | `msw/ws` |
| `sse` | `msw` | `msw/sse` |
| `delay` | `msw` | `msw/utils/delay` |
| `bypass` | `msw` | `msw/utils/bypass` |
| `passthrough` | `msw` | `msw/utils/passthrough` |
| `isCommonAssetRequest` | `msw` | `msw/utils/is-common-asset-request` |

`setupWorker` and `setupServer` stay at `msw/browser` and `msw/node`. React Native moves from the removed `msw/native` entrypoint to the `@msw/react-native` package.

## GraphQL is link-first

`graphql.query()`, `graphql.mutation()` and `graphql.operation()` are removed from the namespace. Create a link per endpoint and define operations on it:

```typescript
// v2
// @ts-expect-error msw 3 does not export graphql from the root; import it from 'msw/graphql'
import { graphql, HttpResponse } from 'msw'

export const handlers = [
  graphql.query('GetUser', () => HttpResponse.json({ data: { user: { name: 'John' } } })),
]
```

```typescript
// v3
import { HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'
import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'

const api = graphql.link('https://api.example.com/graphql')

export const handlers = [
  api.query('GetUser', () => HttpResponse.json({ data: { user: { name: 'John' } } })),
]
```

Links accept relative or absolute URLs, wildcards, and regular expressions. New in v3: `api.subscription()` for GraphQL subscriptions — the resolver receives a `subscription` object with `publish()`.

`msw/graphql` needs the `graphql` package (>=16), now an optional peer dependency of msw. Install it, or the import fails with `Cannot find package 'graphql'`.

## `onUnhandledRequest` → `onUnhandledFrame`

The option on `worker.start()` and `server.listen()` is renamed because it now covers any unhandled **network frame** — requests and WebSocket connections alike:

```typescript
// v3
server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: 'error' })
```

The old name is not an alias. TypeScript rejects `onUnhandledRequest` (TS2353); plain JavaScript ignores it, so the default `'warn'` applies and unhandled requests reach the network without failing anything.

The custom callback shape changed too: it receives a single `{ frame, defaults }` object instead of `(request, print)`. Narrow with `frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame` (from `msw/experimental`) before reading data — a `frame.protocol` check does not narrow the type — and call a method on `defaults` to fall back to a built-in strategy:

```typescript
import { HttpNetworkFrame } from 'msw/experimental'

server.listen({
  onUnhandledFrame({ frame, defaults }) {
    if (frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame && frame.data.request.url.includes('cdn.com')) return
    defaults.warn()
  },
})
```

## Life-cycle events

The `connection` life-cycle event on `server.events` / `worker.events` is renamed:

```typescript
// v2
// @ts-expect-error msw 3 renamed the 'connection' event to 'websocket:connection'
server.events.on('connection', listener)

// v3
server.events.on('websocket:connection', listener)
```

Note: this rename applies to the **life-cycle events API only**. The WebSocket link's own listener — `chat.addEventListener('connection', ...)` — keeps the name `connection`.

The `LifeCycleEventsMap` type is no longer exported from `msw`. Events are described by two per-protocol maps exported from `msw/experimental`:

- `HttpNetworkFrameEventMap` — `request:*`, `response:*`, `unhandledException`
- `WebSocketNetworkFrameEventMap` — `websocket:connection`, `websocket:error`, `graphql:subscription`

Map values changed shape: each key now maps to an event class whose data (`request`, `requestId`, `response`…) is exposed as instance properties. Listeners that destructure those properties keep working unchanged.

## `worker.stop()` returns a Promise

```typescript
// v3 — resolves once interception is disabled for the current client
await worker.stop()
```

## `handleRequest()` removed

`handleRequest()` is no longer exported. For the common case, use the simpler `getResponse()`, which accepts handlers and a request and resolves to a mocked response:

```typescript
// v3
import { getResponse } from 'msw'

const response = await getResponse(handlers, request)
```

If you used `handleRequest` to build a custom interception layer, look at the experimental `defineNetwork()` API instead.

## Path matching moved to `@msw/url`

msw 3.0.0 replaced `path-to-regexp` with its own matcher, `@msw/url`. Two results of this change are
not in the msw migration guide. Both were measured with the same handlers on msw 2.15.0 and msw 3.0.3.

**A repeating path parameter is one string, not an array.**

| Handler | Request | v2 `params` | v3 `params` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/settings/:segments+` | `/settings/user/privacy` | `{ segments: ['user', 'privacy'] }` | `{ segments: 'user/privacy' }` |
| `/files/:path*` | `/files/a/b/c.txt` | `{ path: ['a', 'b', 'c.txt'] }` | `{ path: 'a/b/c.txt' }` |

The `PathParams` type still allows `ReadonlyArray<string>`, so TypeScript does not report v2 code
such as `params.segments.join('/')`. On v3 that call throws a `TypeError` at runtime. The msw docs
page on path parameters still shows arrays. Code that must run on both versions:

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'

http.get('/settings/:segments+', ({ params }) => {
  const segments = [params.segments ?? []].flat().join('/') // 'user/privacy' on v2 and v3
  return HttpResponse.json({ segments })
})
```

**RegExp tokens inside a string predicate do not match.** In v2, `'/user/:id(\\d+)'` matched
`/user/123`. In v3 the same handler matches no request, and the request goes to the unhandled-request
strategy. Use a `RegExp` predicate. Its capture groups arrive by index:

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'

http.get(/\/user\/(\d+)$/, ({ params }) => {
  return HttpResponse.json({ id: params['0'] }) // '123' for /user/123
})
```

## Additional behavior changes (from the release notes)

- Cookies are no longer managed in Node.js; your environment's default applies (browser unaffected). `request.headers.get('cookie')` returns null in handlers — use the `cookies` resolver argument.
- MSW no longer patches `setTimeout` to circumvent fake timers — advance fake timers explicitly.
- `file://` requests and HTTP-to-WebSocket upgrades via `fetch()` throw in Node.js.
- `bypass()` removes the `Content-Length` request header.

## New in v3

- **Vite plugin** at `msw/vite` — serves the worker script for you (no more copying `mockServiceWorker.js` into public) and exposes a preconfigured network via the `virtual:msw` module:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { msw } from 'msw/vite'

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [msw()] })
```

- **GraphQL v17** support and **GraphQL subscriptions**.
- **WebSocket Extension API** for custom experiences, plus the `websocket:error` life-cycle event.
- **Page-navigation and form-submission interception.**
- **Passthrough request-header modification.**
- Node.js v24 and v26 support; TypeScript v6 and v7 support.

## Migration checklist

1. Confirm your runtime: ESM-only project, Node.js >=22, TypeScript >=5.9.
2. Move imports to the subpath entrypoints (`msw/http`, `msw/graphql`, `msw/ws`, `msw/sse`, `msw/utils/*`). Consider the official codemods.
3. React Native: switch `msw/native` imports to `@msw/react-native`.
4. GraphQL: install the `graphql` package, and convert namespace-level `graphql.query/mutation/operation` calls to link-first (`graphql.link(url)` + `link.query(...)`).
5. Rename every `onUnhandledRequest` to `onUnhandledFrame` (JavaScript ignores the old name without a warning); update custom callbacks to the `{ frame, defaults }` shape.
6. Rename the life-cycle `connection` event to `websocket:connection` (the `ws` link's own `addEventListener('connection')` stays as-is).
7. Replace `handleRequest()` with `getResponse()` (or experimental `defineNetwork()` for custom networks).
8. Replace `LifeCycleEventsMap` imports with the per-protocol maps from `msw/experimental`.
9. `await worker.stop()` where shutdown ordering matters.
10. If you relied on MSW handling fake timers or cookie headers in Node, make both explicit in tests.
11. Search for repeating path parameters (`:name+`, `:name*`) and treat their value as a string. Replace RegExp tokens in string predicates (`:id(\\d+)`) with a `RegExp` predicate.

## setupServer (Node.js)

```typescript
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node'
import { handlers } from './handlers'

const server = setupServer(...handlers)
```

Used for Node.js environments: test runners (Vitest, Jest), scripts, and server-side applications.

## setupWorker (Browser)

```typescript
import { setupWorker } from 'msw/browser'
import { handlers } from './handlers'

const worker = setupWorker(...handlers)
```

Used for browser environments: development servers, Storybook, browser-based tests.

## Server Methods

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `.listen(options?)` | Start intercepting requests |
| `.close()` | Stop intercepting, clean up |
| `.use(...handlers)` | Prepend runtime handlers (override) |
| `.resetHandlers(...handlers?)` | Remove runtime handlers, optionally replace initial handlers |
| `.restoreHandlers()` | Mark used one-time handlers as unused again |
| `.listHandlers()` | Return array of all active handlers |
| `.boundary(callback)` | Create isolated handler scope for concurrent tests |
| `.events` | EventEmitter for lifecycle events |

### .listen()

```typescript
server.listen()

// With options
server.listen({
  onUnhandledFrame: 'error',
})
```

### .close()

```typescript
server.close()
```

### .use()

Prepends runtime handlers that take priority over initial handlers:

```typescript
server.use(
  http.get('/api/user', () => HttpResponse.json({ name: 'Override' }))
)
```

Runtime handlers are checked first (most recently added wins). They are removed by `resetHandlers()`.

### .resetHandlers()

```typescript
// Remove all runtime handlers, keep initial handlers
server.resetHandlers()

// Replace initial handlers entirely
server.resetHandlers(
  http.get('/api/user', () => HttpResponse.json({ name: 'New default' }))
)
```

### .restoreHandlers()

Restores one-time handlers that have already been used so they can fire again:

```typescript
server.restoreHandlers()
```

### .listHandlers()

```typescript
const handlers = server.listHandlers()
console.log(handlers.length)
```

## Worker Methods

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `.start(options?)` | Register service worker, start intercepting |
| `.stop()` | Disable mocking for the current client (does NOT unregister the worker) |
| `.use(...handlers)` | Same as server |
| `.resetHandlers()` | Same as server |
| `.restoreHandlers()` | Same as server |
| `.listHandlers()` | Same as server |

### .start()

```typescript
await worker.start()

// With options
await worker.start({
  onUnhandledFrame: 'error',
  serviceWorker: {
    url: '/mockServiceWorker.js',
  },
  quiet: true, // suppress "[MSW] Mocking enabled" console message
})
```

### .stop()

```typescript
worker.stop()
```

`worker.stop()` is not a true opposite of `worker.start()`. It does **not** unregister the service worker — it instructs the worker to disable API mocking for the current client (page) only, which is what allows multiple open clients to hold different interception states. The stopped state does **not** survive a page reload; reloading resumes mocking.

## Lifecycle Events

7 event types available on `server.events` / `worker.events`:

| Event | Payload | Description |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `request:start` | `{ request, requestId }` | Request intercepted |
| `request:match` | `{ request, requestId }` | Handler found |
| `request:unhandled` | `{ request, requestId }` | No handler found |
| `request:end` | `{ request, requestId }` | Request processing done |
| `response:mocked` | `{ request, requestId, response }` | Mocked response sent |
| `response:bypass` | `{ request, requestId, response }` | Real response received |
| `unhandledException` | `{ request, requestId, error }` | Handler threw error |

### Subscribing to events

```typescript
server.events.on('request:start', ({ request, requestId }) => {
  console.log('Intercepted:', request.method, request.url)
})

server.events.on('response:mocked', ({ request, response }) => {
  console.log('Mocked:', request.url, response.status)
})

server.events.on('unhandledException', ({ request, error }) => {
  console.error('Handler error for', request.url, error)
})
```

### Clone before reading body

```typescript
// BAD: consumes the request body, breaking downstream handlers
server.events.on('request:start', async ({ request }) => {
  const body = await request.json()
})

// GOOD: clone before reading
server.events.on('request:start', async ({ request }) => {
  const body = await request.clone().json()
})
```

### Removing event listeners

```typescript
const listener = ({ request }: { request: Request }) => {
  console.log(request.url)
}

server.events.on('request:start', listener)
server.events.removeListener('request:start', listener)

// Or remove all listeners
server.events.removeAllListeners()
```

## onUnhandledFrame Strategies

| Strategy | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| `'warn'` (default) | Console warning, request passes through |
| `'error'` | Console error; the request fails with a network error (`TypeError`) |
| `'bypass'` | Silent, request passes through |
| Custom function | Conditional handling |

**Built-in asset exemption:** for the string strategies, MSW first checks `isCommonAssetRequest(request)` and silently ignores common static asset requests, so they are never treated as unhandled. These never warn or error.

### Built-in strategies

```typescript
server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: 'warn' })   // default
server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: 'error' })   // recommended for tests
server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: 'bypass' })  // silent passthrough
```

### Custom strategy

v3 changed the callback shape: a single `{ frame, defaults }` object instead of `(request, print)`. Narrow with `frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame` (from `msw/experimental`) before reading `frame.data` — a `frame.protocol` check does not narrow its type — and call a method on `defaults` (`defaults.warn()`, `defaults.error()`) to use a built-in strategy.

```typescript
import { HttpNetworkFrame } from 'msw/experimental'
import { isCommonAssetRequest } from 'msw/utils/is-common-asset-request'

server.listen({
  onUnhandledFrame({ frame, defaults }) {
    // Supplying a custom callback OPTS OUT of MSW's built-in
    // common-asset exemption — re-apply it manually.
    if (frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame && isCommonAssetRequest(frame.data.request)) {
      return
    }

    if (frame instanceof HttpNetworkFrame) {
      const url = new URL(frame.data.request.url)
      if (url.hostname === 'cdn.example.com') {
        return
      }
    }

    defaults.error()
  },
})
```

## server.boundary()

Isolates handler scope for parallel execution. Handlers added via `server.use()` inside a boundary are only visible within that boundary's execution context.

```typescript
const isolated = server.boundary(async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/user', () => HttpResponse.json({ role: 'admin' }))
  )
  // This override is only visible within this boundary
})

await isolated()
```

### Use with concurrent tests

```typescript
it.concurrent('admin flow', server.boundary(async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/me', () => HttpResponse.json({ role: 'admin' }))
  )
  // Only this test sees the admin override
}))

it.concurrent('guest flow', server.boundary(async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/me', () => HttpResponse.json({ role: 'guest' }))
  )
  // Only this test sees the guest override
}))
```

# Use v2 Destructured Resolver Signature

## Problem

v1 used `(req, res, ctx) => res(ctx.json(...))`. v2 uses a single info object with `request`, `params`, `cookies`. Using the v1 signature causes runtime errors.

## Incorrect

```typescript
// BUG: v1 resolver signature — does not work in v2
// @ts-expect-error v2 resolvers take one info object, not (req, res, ctx)
http.get('/api/user/:id', (req, res, ctx) => {
  const { id } = req.params
  return res(ctx.json({ id, name: 'John' }))
})
```

## Correct

```typescript
// v2 resolver receives a single info object
http.get('/api/user/:id', ({ request, params, cookies }) => {
  const { id } = params
  return HttpResponse.json({ id, name: 'John' })
})
```

## Resolver Info Properties

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `request` | `Request` | Standard Fetch API Request object |
| `params` | `Record<string, string \| string[]>` | Path parameters. In msw 3.0.3 a repeating param (`:segments+`, `:path*`) arrives as one string with its slashes (`'a/b'`); the docs and the type also allow an array |
| `cookies` | `Record<string, string>` | Parsed request cookies |
| `requestId` | `string` | Unique request identifier |
| `finalize` | `Function` | Schedule a cleanup callback to run after the resolver completes |

## Why

v2 aligns with web standards. The resolver receives a Fetch API `Request` object instead of MSW's custom `req`. Responses are standard `Response` objects (or `HttpResponse`), not composed via `res(ctx.*)`.

# Use `HttpResponse` Static Methods Instead of `res(ctx.*)`

## Problem

v1 response composition `res(ctx.status(200), ctx.json(...))` doesn't exist in v2. Responses are now standard Response objects constructed via `HttpResponse`.

## Incorrect

```typescript
// BUG: res() and ctx are removed in v2
// @ts-expect-error v2 resolvers take one info object, not (req, res, ctx)
http.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) => {
  return res(
    ctx.status(200),
    ctx.json({ name: 'John' }),
    ctx.set('X-Custom', 'value'),
  )
})
```

## Correct

```typescript
http.get('/api/user', () => {
  return HttpResponse.json(
    { name: 'John' },
    {
      status: 200,
      headers: { 'X-Custom': 'value' },
    },
  )
})
```

## v1 to v2 Response Mapping

| v1 Pattern | v2 Equivalent |
|-----------|---------------|
| `res(ctx.json(data))` | `HttpResponse.json(data)` |
| `res(ctx.text(str))` | `HttpResponse.text(str)` |
| `res(ctx.xml(str))` | `HttpResponse.xml(str)` |
| `res(ctx.status(code))` | `new HttpResponse(null, { status: code })` |
| `res(ctx.set(name, val))` | `new HttpResponse(body, { headers: { [name]: val } })` |
| `res(ctx.delay(ms), ...)` | `await delay(ms); return HttpResponse.json(...)` |
| `res(ctx.cookie(name, val))` | `HttpResponse.json(data, { headers: { 'Set-Cookie': '...' } })` |
| `res.networkError(msg)` | `HttpResponse.error()` |
| `res.once(...)` | `http.get(url, resolver, { once: true })` |

## Why

v2 aligns with the Fetch API standard. `HttpResponse` extends the native `Response` class, making mock responses consistent with real responses and enabling features like `Set-Cookie` header support.

# Clone Request Before Reading Body in Lifecycle Events

## Problem

When you read `request.json()` in a lifecycle event listener like `request:start`, the body stream is consumed. MSW can then no longer clone the request for the handler lookup: the lookup fails with `TypeError: unusable`, MSW logs "Encountered an unhandled exception during the handler lookup", and the client receives a 500 response instead of the mock.

## Incorrect

```typescript
// BUG: reading the body consumes the stream — the handler lookup fails and the client gets a 500
server.events.on('request:start', async ({ request }) => {
  const body = await request.json()
  console.log('Request body:', body)
})
```

## Correct

```typescript
server.events.on('request:start', async ({ request }) => {
  const clone = request.clone()
  const body = await clone.json()
  console.log('Request body:', body)
})
```

## Why

The Fetch API `Request` body is a `ReadableStream` — once read, it's consumed. Lifecycle events share the same `Request` object with handlers. Cloning creates an independent copy with its own body stream, so reading in the event listener doesn't interfere with handler resolution.

# Import Server/Worker from Correct Subpaths

## Problem

Developers import `setupServer` from `'msw'` instead of `'msw/node'`. The root `'msw'` module does not export `setupServer` or `setupWorker`.

## Incorrect

```typescript
// BUG: setupServer is not exported from 'msw'
// @ts-expect-error setupServer is exported from 'msw/node', not 'msw'
import { setupServer } from 'msw'
```

## Correct

```typescript
// Node.js (tests, SSR)
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node'

// Browser (Storybook, development)
import { setupWorker } from 'msw/browser'

// Handlers and response utilities come from 'msw/http' (v3 subpath)
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw/http'
import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'
```

## Import Map

| Export | Import from |
|--------|-------------|
| `http`, `HttpResponse` | `'msw/http'` |
| `graphql` | `'msw/graphql'` (install the `graphql` package) |
| `ws`, `sse` | `'msw/ws'`, `'msw/sse'` |
| `delay`, `bypass`, `passthrough` | `'msw/utils/delay'`, `'msw/utils/bypass'`, `'msw/utils/passthrough'` |
| `setupServer` | `'msw/node'` |
| `setupWorker` | `'msw/browser'` |
| `setupServer` (React Native) | `'@msw/react-native'` |

## Why

MSW uses subpath exports to tree-shake correctly. Importing `setupServer` from `'msw'` produces an import error. The split ensures browser code doesn't bundle Node.js dependencies and vice versa.

React Native has a third subpath, `'@msw/react-native'`. It exports the same `setupServer` API but ships the interceptors relevant to the React Native environment. `msw/node` pulls in Node.js modules such as `http` that do not exist in React Native, so replace any `msw/node` import in React Native code with `@msw/react-native`.

# Test Application Behavior, Not Request Mechanics

## Problem

Asserting that `fetch` was called with specific arguments tests implementation details, not behavior. If the app switches from `fetch` to `axios`, the test breaks even though behavior is identical.

## Incorrect

```tsx
// BUG: testing implementation, not behavior
test('logs in the user', async () => {
  render(<LoginForm />)
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('Email'), 'john@test.com')
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('Password'), 'password')
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }))

  // Fragile: tests HOW the app fetches, not WHAT happens
  expect(fetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/api/login', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'john@test.com', password: 'password' }),
  })
})
```

## Correct

```tsx
test('logs in the user', async () => {
  render(<LoginForm />)
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('Email'), 'john@test.com')
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('Password'), 'password')
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }))

  // Tests WHAT the user sees after login
  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(screen.getByText('Welcome, John!')).toBeInTheDocument()
  })
})
```

## Why

MSW intercepts requests at the network level, so your tests should focus on observable outcomes: what the user sees, what state changes, what the function returns. This makes tests resilient to HTTP client refactors and more readable.

Where the request's *validity* is what you care about, validate it inside the handler and return an error response for a bad request. Upstream puts it this way: "Not only is this the right way to assert the request's validity, error handling also brings your request handlers closer to the production behavior."

**Exception:** some requests leave no observable trace in the application — typically one-way calls to third-party services such as analytics or monitoring. For those, use the life-cycle events API (`server.events.on('request:start', ...)`, see `references/server-api.md`) to assert on requests directly.
